instruction: Compare the original and rewrite directly. Independently identify substantive reasoning relations in the original and check all against the rewrite, including omissions, additions, conditions, timing, actors, causal direction, and scope. Return status preserved only when all substantive reasoning survives. Use changed for a material change and uncertain for unresolved meaning. Give concrete evidence for your assessment. Wording and presentation order may differ.

documents.original:
The lawn slopes gently toward the changing rooms. Put the screen at the low end so people sitting on a blanket can see over the row ahead. At dusk the west-facing windows throw a bright reflection across the picnic ground. A projection test at the actual show time will reveal whether the screen needs to shift a few feet. Families bringing toddlers often leave before the credits. Reserve blanket space beside the exit path so those departures do not set off a chain of people standing up. Pool loungers sit much higher than picnic rugs. Mark a chair area behind the blankets while there is still daylight and late arrivals will know where they can unfold a seat.

The grass between the gate and the picnic tables gets soft after watering. Set aside viewing places along the paved strip so wheelchair users can sit with their friends. The snack counter normally takes cash from members. Print prices and payment methods on the invitation so a family can bring the right change or pack its own picnic. Several nearby homes face the lawn across a narrow lane. Aim the speakers into the audience and listen from the lane during the sound check to catch dialogue that carries into bedrooms. Even on a quiet evening, wind can swallow a softly spoken line. Turn on captions and have somebody read them from the back row before admitting guests.

For someone arriving alone, a full lawn can look like a collection of private parties. Have a greeter keep track of gaps and offer to show newcomers an open spot. A small child looking for a parent may remember the striped snack awning more easily than a volunteer's name. Introduce it as the meeting place during the welcome. A streaming subscription may cover only household viewing. Secure permission for the outdoor screening before announcing the title so the club can advertise a film it can actually show. The club secretary has to return borrowed gear the next morning. Keep its packing boxes together with the lenders' names so teardown volunteers can put the right remote and cables back with each machine.
documents.rewrite:
Before putting a film title on the invitation, get the rights holder's go-ahead for showing it outdoors. The club's streaming account might only cover watching at home. Tell families what the refreshments will cost and how they can pay. Regulars may know to take cash to the snack counter, but a first-time visitor would appreciate the chance to bring change or make a picnic instead.

Try out the projector at the hour the film will start. The downhill end of the lawn by the changing rooms gives people on rugs a view over those in front, but the glare off the west-facing windows at dusk could make it worth moving the screen a little. While it's light, mark out the space at the back for loungers and other chairs. That way even the last person in with a folding seat will know where to go without blocking the view from a rug. Leave room for blankets by the way out for families who may take a toddler home early, so other people can stay seated. Watering leaves the ground from the gate to the picnic tables soft. Save spots for wheelchair users and their companions together along the paving.

Check the film from both sides of the lawn before opening up. Someone at the back should be able to read the captions when the breeze makes a quiet exchange hard to hear. Point the speakers toward the crowd and walk out into the narrow lane at sound check to hear how much of the conversation might reach the bedrooms opposite. Once people arrive, a greeter who knows which spaces are free can walk a solo guest over to one, even if every group looks like a private gathering. During the welcome, point out the striped awning over the snack counter as the place to meet if anyone gets separated. A child can pick that out without having to remember an unfamiliar name. Put the lenders' names on the equipment boxes and keep all the boxes in one place. The people clearing up can reunite each machine with its own leads and remote in time for the secretary's returns the following morning.

documents.original:
People may bring a sewing machine expecting a sewing volunteer to repair the motor. Describe a few jobs the volunteers can actually tackle in the invitation so residents can judge whether to make the trip. A photograph of a broken hinge tells a woodworker more than the booking note 'cabinet trouble.' Invite people to send a picture ahead of time so the volunteer can bring the right clamps. Carrying a broken lamp across town is work in itself. Remind people to bring its shade, fittings and any loose pieces so a missing part does not prevent a repair. Screws from two radios look much alike once they are on a crowded table. Give each job its own shallow tray so the parts and the owner's belongings travel together.

Threading a needle is difficult under the hall's high ceiling lights. Put a movable task lamp on the sewing table so the volunteer and the garment's owner can see the stitch clearly. The hall's folding tables wobble when somebody leans on a vise. Assign clamping jobs to the solid workbench so the neighboring repairer can work without tools creeping toward the edge. A visitor holding a heavy toaster should not have to queue on their feet. Take their name at the door and give them a seat within earshot of the person calling jobs. A worn jacket may carry more sentimental value than its owner mentions at first. Show the proposed patch against the fabric and get their agreement before making a visible alteration.

When a volunteer does every stitch, the same loose button will bring its owner back. Let the visitor finish the last few stitches with guidance so they leave knowing how to repeat the mend. Battery compartments sometimes arrive with obvious leaks. Ask the intake volunteer to flag those items before they reach the shared work surface so the session lead can arrange appropriate handling. If an owner goes home for a missing attachment, another volunteer may inherit the repair. Tie a short work note to the handle so the next person can pick up at the right point. Fifteen minutes before the hall closes, opening another clock creates a tableful of parts with nowhere to go. Switch intake to advice and future bookings while the current jobs are wrapped up.
documents.rewrite:
Make it possible to decide at home whether a trip to the hall is worthwhile. Give examples of repairs the volunteers know how to do. Someone who sees sewing on the bill might otherwise haul over a machine with a broken motor. Offer to look at photos in advance. A woodworker who can see which cupboard hinge has broken has a much better chance of bringing the right clamps. Ask people to pack everything that goes with the item, down to a lamp's shade, fittings and pieces that have come off. It would be a pity to carry it all that way and be unable to fix it for want of one piece.

At the door, take the owner's name and find them somewhere to sit where they can hear their turn called, especially if they're carrying something heavy like a toaster. Have the person receiving items watch for visible battery leaks and tell the lead before the item goes onto a communal table, so the lead can decide how to handle it. Give each repair its own low-sided tray and keep it with the owner's things. Two opened radios can yield screws that are almost impossible to tell apart. If someone has to fetch an attachment from home, fasten a brief account of the work so far to the handle in case a different volunteer takes over.

Do the vise work on the sturdy bench. The folding tables rock under pressure and the person working alongside could see their tools slide off. At the sewing station, give the owner and the volunteer an adjustable light close enough to see the needle and the stitching, since the overhead lights are a long way up. Hold a patch against a jacket and let the owner approve the look before sewing it on. They may care a great deal about that jacket even if they haven't said so. On a simple mend such as a loose button, talk them through sewing the last stitches themselves so they can do it next time. With a quarter of an hour left, offer advice or book the next visit while people finish what they've started. That's a better time to discuss someone's clock than to take it apart and run out of time to put it back together.

documents.original:
Afternoon sun heats the catalog under the front window. Move it to the cooler interior wall so the contents are less likely to deteriorate while waiting for planting season. Gardeners call the same bean by several local names. Put those names on the drawer card beside the variety name so neighbors can recognize the seed they came looking for. A donated jar can contain enough lettuce seed for dozens of gardens. Portion it into small envelopes at a packing afternoon so the first visitor can take a useful amount without emptying the supply. Gardeners may know when they picked a tomato without remembering when they saved the seed. Ask for the harvest year at donation and mark uncertain dates clearly so borrowers can judge older stock.

One community gardener has noticed which beds stay frosty well into spring. Invite her to annotate the sowing calendar with local observations so the printed dates make sense on nearby streets. Seeds sold for ornamental use sometimes come with a coating the library cannot identify. Ask donors for the original label and have staff check it before accepting commercial leftovers. Seeds saved from a supermarket squash may grow quite differently from the parent. Give uncertain parentage a plain-language note so growers who need predictable results can choose another packet. New gardeners sometimes pull up a seedling with the weeds. Ask local growers for pictures of the first leaves and display them beside the cabinet to help visitors recognize what emerges.

A whole drawer of free seed may tempt a visitor to take more than they can plant. Print the approximate number of pots or row length on the label so they can choose enough for their space. The peas that disappear first might simply be the easiest packet to see. Compare the tally with drawer positions before asking donors to devote more of their gardens to that variety. Some neighbors would happily save seed but pick every pod for dinner. Put a reminder out before harvest explaining which plants to leave standing so donors still have mature seed to bring in. An interesting growing note can get lost when a packet changes hands. Keep a notebook near the drawers where borrowers can record how that variety fared on a windy balcony or in heavy soil.
documents.rewrite:
Give the seeds a cool place to wait for planting time. The cabinet against an inside wall will keep better than it does in the heat of the afternoon window. When someone brings in seed, ask which year's crop it came from. They may remember picking the tomatoes better than saving the seed, and a clearly marked doubtful date lets people make their own call about an older packet. For leftover commercial seed, get the original package label and let library staff check it before taking the donation. Some ornamental seed has a coating that's hard to identify by sight. A seed from a shop-bought squash might grow into something quite unlike it. Explain in everyday language when the parentage is uncertain, so someone counting on a particular crop can pick something else.

Get a few neighbors together for an afternoon of packing. A jar of lettuce seed will go round dozens of plots if it's divided into envelopes before the first person arrives. Say roughly how many pots or how much of a row an envelope will sow. It's easier to take only what you can use, even with a whole drawer on offer for free. On the drawer card, include the neighborhood's different names for a bean along with its variety name, so a gardener looking for an old favorite knows where it is.

Let visitors see what the gardeners have learned. Put pictures from local growers beside the drawers showing the very first leaves, when it's easiest for someone starting out to weed out the plant they meant to keep. Ask the gardener who knows where the frost lingers to add her observations to the sowing calendar. A date on the page then means something to someone planting a few streets away. Leave a notebook there too, where borrowers can say which variety did well in heavy ground or on an exposed balcony. The observation will stay available after the packet moves on.

Send a reminder before harvest about which plants need to be left to mature. Someone happy to contribute next year's seed might otherwise eat every pod. When using the pickup count to ask for more seed, first look at where the varieties sit in the cabinet. Growers needn't give extra space to the first peas to run out if those happened to be the packets everybody could see.

documents.original:
The delivery van and the younger pupils use the same side gate. Agree on a delivery window before the first class comes outside so staff can unload without children weaving around the trolley. The assembly hall has a raised threshold that is barely noticeable on foot. Push a loaded trolley along the delivery route before opening day to find where a ramp or another entrance is needed. The cooking school needs numbers before its pots go on. Have the office send attendance changes at an agreed morning cutoff so the cooks can adjust portions while there is still time. Several children receive individualized meals that look much like the standard dish. Have the designated adult match each covered portion with the child's meal record before bringing it to their place.

The hall has one handwashing station near the stage. Let each class wash at its usual sinks on the way down so the lunch queue can keep moving once children arrive. On wet days coats make narrow aisles even tighter. Keep the usual classroom pegs in use for lunch so children carrying trays have a clear path between tables. The smallest children cannot see into the serving pans. Display a photo of the day's plate where the line begins so they can recognize what's on offer before reaching the server. A child juggling a cup and a tray may spill both on the turn into the hall. Put water jugs on the tables so pupils can sit down before pouring a drink.

Some children normally eat in a quieter corner of the dining room. Set a table away from the trolley and loudspeaker so they can keep that part of their lunchtime routine. Wheelchair users can approach the tables along the central aisle yet still find every end blocked by a bench. Leave accessible places among classmates when laying out the furniture each morning. The hall is needed for afternoon music, and stacked tables can block the instrument cupboard. Mark parking places for furniture with the music teacher so the room is ready for the next lesson. The final delivery crates will still belong to the lending school when the kitchen reopens. Count them against the delivery log during the last collection so staff know what has gone home.
documents.rewrite:
Walk the food in once before the first lunch, with the trolley carrying its usual load. The little step into the assembly hall feels quite different with wheels under that much weight, and staff can decide in advance whether to put down a ramp or use a different door. Book the van in early enough to unload at the shared side gate before the youngest class comes out. Agree a morning deadline with the school doing the cooking, and have the office tell them about changes in attendance by then, while they can still change how many portions they cook.

Use the children's familiar route where it helps. Each class can leave coats on its own pegs, even on rainy days, and wash hands at the sinks it normally uses on the way to lunch. Children with trays get more room in the aisles, and one basin by the stage won't have to serve a whole queue. Put a picture of that day's meal at the start of the line. Small pupils can see what to ask for even if they can't see over the serving dishes. For individual meals, give one designated adult the job of checking each covered dish against the child's record before taking it to the child's seat. Several could easily pass for the ordinary lunch.

As the tables go out each morning, leave room for wheelchair users to sit with their class. The central passage may be perfectly clear and still lead to a row of tables with benches across every end. Pick a table clear of both the loudspeaker and the delivery trolley for children accustomed to a quiet lunch. Leave jugs of water on the tables so pupils can put down their trays and sit before getting a drink. Carrying a filled cup around the turn into the hall makes an extra spill likely.

Get the music teacher to help mark where the stacked furniture goes after lunch. The afternoon class needs to be able to get into the instrument cupboard as soon as the room is handed back. When the six weeks are up, use the delivery record to check off the crates as the other school collects them for the last time, so everyone knows which ones made it back.

documents.original:
The groundskeeper knows when the sprinklers start and which gates get locked. Agree on an observing area and departure time with them before putting either detail on the invitation. The Moon gives a beginner something recognizable to find with the naked eye. Choose a night when a crescent or quarter Moon will stand above the local roofline during the gathering. Clouds often leave people wondering whether to set off from home. Give the invitation a specific time and place for the go-ahead message, with a reserve evening listed alongside it. A sign that points across a lawn is little help to someone pushing a wheelchair or a buggy. Trace the firm route from the entrance and describe its distance, surface and tightest turn in the invitation.

New arrivals naturally look for the busiest spot and can blunder into a tripod. Put the greeting point on the approach path and have someone show them where the telescope legs begin. Finding a constellation becomes easier when the paper turns with the viewer. Mark one conspicuous landmark on a simple chart so people can line up the page from their actual starting position. A telescope pointed at nothing in particular makes a poor first demonstration. Have its lender align the finder before dusk so the volunteer can return quickly to a target after an accidental bump. A family waiting behind one observer can feel pressured to take a single hurried glance. Hand out return slips at the telescope so people can explore the sky nearby until their turn comes around.

An invitation to notice one detail gives quiet visitors a way into the conversation. Leave pencils and small cards for people to sketch the boundary between the Moon's lit and shaded portions. Standing on grass feels colder than walking there, especially for an observer waiting a turn. Mention warm layers in the invitation and place a few seats on the sheltered edge of the observing area. Sound carries beyond the common after dusk. Gather small groups close to their guide so directions can be given in a conversational voice that also leaves other observers free to listen. The last observers still need light to leave while volunteers are packing. Assign one volunteer to stay at the gate with a shielded light until everyone and both instruments have reached the path.
documents.rewrite:
Pick a date when people can find a crescent or quarter Moon for themselves above the neighborhood roofs during the event. Before printing the invitations, settle the spot and finishing time with the groundskeeper, who knows the watering times and when the gates close. Give people a fallback date and tell them exactly where and when to check whether clouds have called off the first evening. Walk the firm way in and put the distance, surface and sharpest turn in the invitation so someone bringing a wheelchair or buggy can judge the route. Pointing across the grass doesn't tell them how to get there. Suggest warm layers, too. Waiting on grass gets chilly much faster than walking across it. A few chairs on the sheltered side will be welcome.

Have the lender set up the finder before daylight fades, so even if the telescope gets knocked the volunteer can quickly put something worth seeing back in view. Meet people on the path on their way in and point out the tripod feet before they head straight for the crowd. Give them a simple map of the stars with an unmistakable local landmark on it. They can turn the chart to match where they're standing, which makes finding a constellation much easier.

Give out slips at the telescopes that let people come back for their turns. Families will have time to look around for themselves, and the person at the eyepiece won't have a line of people waiting for them to finish a hurried peek. Put out cards and pencils and suggest drawing the line between light and dark on the Moon. Noticing that one feature gives a shy visitor something specific to talk about. Keep each group near its guide so nobody needs to shout instructions. Voices travel after dark, and people using the other telescope will want to hear as well. At pack-up time, leave a volunteer at the gate with a shaded light until the last guest and both telescopes are safely on the path. People leaving late still need to see their way out.

documents.original:
A whole district is difficult to hold in mind on a short walk. Build the route around how the neighborhood uses the river and let each stop reveal a different answer in a resident's voice. The river can be busy enough to drown out the best line in an interview. Test listening positions at the time visitors are likely to walk and move a stop inland if its speech disappears. A visitor following an interview may walk right past the building it describes. Open each stop with one precise visual cue and ask listeners to settle there before the story begins. A row of nearly identical warehouses invites wrong turns. Photograph the distinctive end wall from the direction of travel and reuse that viewpoint on the map where the turn occurs.

A resident's memory lands differently when listeners can inspect something it mentions. Ask interviewees to bring the interviewer to a surviving detail, then record what they notice while standing beside it. An interview may include a family story its speaker later wants to keep private. Play the edited extract to the speaker and agree on its wording, credit and public use before including it. Spoken directions can sound obvious at a desk and fail within seconds on the street. Give an early cut to a newcomer, walk a few paces behind and note where they have to look back. A long street name can be hard to recognize when heard only once. Pair stop titles with the same plain place names on the map, player and direction signs that a visitor will consult.

A visitor who needs a rest should be able to judge how far remains. Mark verified benches and the distance to the next stop on the map, including stretches with nowhere to sit. When a path closes temporarily, a printed arrow can send people to a locked gate. Keep a dated route notice on the tour page with an alternate approach to the affected stop. Not everyone wants to install an app for a half-hour walk. Give the tour a short, readable web address on the starting notice so someone can type it or share it aloud. A listener who knows the area may spot a mistaken name months after launch. Put a correction contact beside each transcript and ask for the stop title so volunteers can locate the disputed passage.
documents.rewrite:
I'd give a short walk one question to follow through the district. How do the people who live here use the river? Let a different neighbor answer at each stop. While interviewing, ask the speaker to take you to some trace of their story that a walker can still see, and record what catches their attention there. Visitors will be able to look for it as they listen. Play each edited passage back to the person whose voice it is. A family memory they were happy to tell the interviewer may feel private on hearing it again. Settle the wording, how they'll be credited and whether they're happy to go public before you use it.

Listen on location at the hour you expect people to take the tour. If the river traffic blots out the words, bring that stop a little farther inland. Start the recording for each location with a single clear thing to look for and ask the walker to pause there. That gives them a chance to find the building before they get caught up in the interview and pass it. Where the warehouses all look alike, take a picture of the end wall that stands out, as a walker would see it coming up the street. Use that view on the map right at the turn. Keep the place names simple and identical in the stop titles, map, player and signs. Someone who's heard a long street name once may struggle to recognize it later.

Try a rough edit on someone who doesn't know the neighborhood. Follow a short way behind and notice each time they have to look back. A direction that sounds perfectly clear indoors can go wrong as soon as you leave the desk. Visit the benches before marking them and give the distance to the following stop on the map, pointing out any interval without seating so walkers can plan a rest. Put a short web address people can read, type or tell a friend on the starting sign, so a half-hour outing doesn't depend on downloading an app.

Keep a dated update on the tour page with another way to reach a stop if a temporary closure makes the printed arrows point to a shut gate. Beside every transcript, tell readers whom to contact about corrections and ask them to name the stop. If someone who knows the district spots a wrong name months later, a volunteer can still find the exact place in the recording.

documents.original:
An ensemble named on a cover may require an unexpected doubling halfway through. Check the actual parts and list every required instrument alongside any optional substitutions the arrangement provides. A clarinet player may search by the instrument in hand and another player by the key heard in the room. Record the part's transposition separately from the work's concert key so both searches make sense. A beginner can make better use of a concrete difficulty note than an unexplained star rating. Have a player identify features such as shifting meter or sustained high notes that influence rehearsal time. An unfamiliar local composition may find an audience once players hear its shape. When its creator agrees, pair the catalog entry with a short performance excerpt and credit those who made the recording.

Small type on a high shelf is hard to inspect in a busy corridor. Keep a printed browsing binder at seated height and use shelf codes that match the stickers on the music folders. Pieces remembered by an opening line can vanish from a title-only index. Add alternate titles and first lines where available so a half-remembered piece has more than one path to its entry. Loose parts can migrate between near-identical folders after rehearsal. Give each part the same collection code as its folder in a removable sleeve, with the instrument name visible at the top. A quartet loses a rehearsal when the second violin part is missing. Put a parts inventory inside the folder and have the borrower and return volunteer check it at opposite ends of the loan.

Singling out the only borrower of a rare part on a public sign-out sheet can feel intrusive. Keep contact details in the center's private loan record and show only availability in the browsing catalog. An entire group may plan around a score being available on a certain evening. Let a named representative reserve the folder for a rehearsal and display the date it is expected back. Many published bindings resist a music stand and can be damaged by forcing them flat. Provide a stand for trying a score at the center so borrowers can see how the edition sits before taking it away. Several copies of a popular score may be more useful than another copy of a seldom-played arrangement. Count unmet requests by edition and use those figures when asking donors for additions.
documents.rewrite:
Think about what a musician needs to know before committing a group to a piece. Open the folder and look through the parts. An ensemble name on the cover can conceal a change of instrument halfway through, so record every instrument the players will need and any alternatives actually offered in the arrangement. Give the sounding key of the work and the transposition of the individual part their own entries. That helps both the clarinetist searching with an instrument in hand and the musician who remembers the key they heard. Ask somebody who has played the piece to describe the challenges that affect rehearsal time. A beginner can make more of a warning about changing meters or a long high passage than a number of stars. For a little-known local piece, a short sample performance might introduce it to players. Get the composer's agreement and credit the people behind the recording.

Put the printed index where someone sitting down can browse it, away from the problem of reading small print high up in a busy passage. Use the same shelf references in it as on the folder stickers. Include first lines and other titles when you know them, since a musician who can sing the opening might have forgotten its title. Have a music stand available at the center for trying an edition before checking it out. Borrowers can see whether the binding will stay open without having to press it flat and risk damaging it.

Keep every loose part in a removable sleeve bearing the folder's collection code, with the instrument visible at the top. It will be much easier to put each part back where it belongs when several similar folders are out after a rehearsal. Put a checklist inside each folder. Ask the borrower to check the contents on the way out and the volunteer to check on return. Finding out at rehearsal that a quartet is short its second violin part costs all four people an evening.

Let one named member book a folder for the group's rehearsal and let other users see its availability and expected return date. Keep names and contact information in the center's private lending record. Publishing who took a rarely used part could pick out an individual borrower quite easily. Log requests you couldn't fill, including the particular edition requested. When people ask what to donate, those counts will tell you whether another copy of a frequently played score will get more use than a duplicate of one that rarely goes out.

documents.original:
A familiar brand can reuse a box design across several piece counts. Label each donated puzzle with its title and stated count from the manufacturer's panel so people can compare likely commitments. A thousand-piece puzzle with distinct illustrated characters feels different from a thousand pieces of sky. Let contributors add a plain description of the image and the stretches that made their build challenging. People vary in how much a missing piece bothers them. Keep playable incomplete puzzles together and show the known gap on the box image with a removable note so takers can decide. An already assembled jigsaw is easier to take down when large sections are turned over first. Invite the last builder to check the backs and separate connected pieces before donating it for a fresh solve.

People with limited grip may find small, thickly packed pieces awkward to handle. Mark large-piece sets by their actual piece size and keep a sample outline on their cards for comparison. A small child may reach whatever is on the bottom shelf while a caregiver browses. Reserve that space for boxed children's puzzles and keep the original age guidance visible on each one. An image printed on the lid may be the only reference available while assembling. Check that the picture is legible and include a clean image from the donor when a damaged lid needs a substitute. Damp cardboard can spoil the boxes beside it once a cupboard closes. Examine incoming boxes in good light and ask the donor to take back any that show moisture or mildew.

People may forget a puzzle's title by the time they discover a problem at home. Give accepted boxes a short identifier so a resident can report an issue without trying to describe the artwork. When a reported missing piece turns up under the dining table, a whole puzzle can become complete again. Keep found pieces in labeled envelopes behind the desk and match them using the puzzle identifier. Volunteers need a way to tell high turnover from slow accumulation. Tally incoming and outgoing boxes during each opening and use the trend to decide when the next donation window can fit. Neighbors sometimes need to picture a completed puzzle before they choose it. Invite builders to contribute a snapshot for a noticeboard and put its box identifier underneath so someone can look for the same one.
documents.rewrite:
Take a good look at each box in decent light before it joins the cupboard. If there's damp or mildew, ask the donor to take it home, since it could spoil the boxes next to it in a closed space. Make sure the lid picture is clear enough to solve the puzzle from. Sometimes it's the builder's only guide, so ask for a clean image from the donor if the lid is damaged. If the donor still has the puzzle laid out, suggest turning over big sections first. The last builder can check the backs as they take it apart and separate any joined pieces so the next person gets the whole experience.

Copy the title and the manufacturer's stated piece count from the information panel onto the exchange label. The same brand may dress several sizes in much the same box, and people need to judge how long a build they're taking on. Invite the builder to say what the picture shows and where they got stuck. A thousand illustrated figures make for a very different job from a thousand pieces of sky. Put usable puzzles with known missing pieces together and mark the gap on each lid picture with a removable slip. Someone who's fine with a gap can see what they'll be getting.

For a large-piece puzzle, give the actual piece dimensions and put an outline on the card that people can compare. Small pieces crowded together are fiddly for someone with limited grip. Give the lowest shelf to boxed children's puzzles and keep the maker's age advice in view. That's the shelf a little one can reach while the adult is choosing. For people who like to see the finished picture first, invite builders to put a photo on the noticeboard and write the box code below it so the next person can find that particular set.

Assign each box you accept a short code. If a resident notices something wrong at home they've only got to quote the code, even if they can't remember the name or describe the scene. Keep stray pieces in marked envelopes behind the desk. When the piece thought lost is found under someone's table, the code gives you a way to reunite it with its box and make the set whole again. At every opening count boxes taken away as well as those arriving. Watching both figures over time will show whether puzzles are changing hands quickly or quietly piling up, so you can time the next call for donations to the space available.
